structure.title: 称呼[
structure.summary: The partial document discusses regional naming conventions for SARS in Asia, noting that mainland China commonly calls it “非典型肺炎” or “非典,” though not identical to SARS; Hong Kong uses the Cantonese transliteration “沙士” or the English term; Taiwan also uses “SARS”; Malaysian Chinese media uses “SARS”; Singapore’s media initially said “薩斯,” later standardized to “沙斯.”

nodes.title: **爆发初期和隐瞒**[
nodes.summary: Document describes the initial outbreak of SARS in Guangdong, China, beginning Nov 2002. Authorities in Guangdong and Guangzhou withheld information, restricted media, suppressed online discussions. SARS cases spread in several cities—Shunde, Heyuan, Zhongshan, Foshan, Guangzhou—prompting investigation by Guangdong health authorities. They issued reports and alerts (Jan 23, Feb 3) naming disease “atypical pneumonia” and urging control measures. Outbreak peaked early Feb with rising cases (218 by Feb 6), including many healthcare workers. Chinese Ministry of Health involved Feb 9. Public panic led to runs on preventive items like banlangen and vinegar, prices spiking dramatically.

nodes.title: **疫情公开后**[
nodes.summary: Details the initial public disclosure of the SARS outbreak in Guangdong in February 2003, covering official announcements to WHO and the public, media reports on case numbers and fatalities, government press conferences and explanations for delayed reporting, expert briefings on transmission and school reopening, national health authorities’ risk assessments, continuation of major public events like football matches and concerts due to perceived limited risk, and updates from the Chinese CDC on laboratory assessments and the reported case count.

nodes.title: **传播扩散**[
nodes.summary: Partial document discusses SARS spread starting Feb 21 2003 when Liu Jianlun brought virus to Hong Kong, infected many via hotel transmission leading to outbreaks in hospitals and communities (Prince of Wales Hospital, Amoy Gardens). Details numerous transmission chains, hospital outbreaks, global spread to Vietnam, Singapore, Canada etc., WHO warnings, naming of SARS, cases in China including Beijing, government responses, misinformation, eventual admission and cooperation with WHO, media coverage, internal criticism from Jiang Yanyong, removal of health minister.

nodes.title: **大规模公开防疫**[
nodes.summary: The document details how China faced international scrutiny following the SARS outbreak, leading to cooperation with WHO investigations in early April 2003. It chronicles the escalating crisis in Beijing and other regions, including coverups, public events undertaken to demonstrate control, the rapid rise in cases, and subsequent containment measures like appointing WHO teams, imposing “one-day reporting” on SARS statistics, travel restrictions, cancellation of large gatherings, suspension of schools and so-called “Golden Week,” and construction of dedicated hospitals such as Xiaotangshan. High-level political actions are noted: leadership meetings, warnings against underreporting, and removal of Beijing’s mayor and China’s health minister, replaced by Wang Qishan and Wu Yi. The text also describes government mandates like cremating SARS victims, halting sports events, restricting travel, provisioning emergency funds, and ensuring police maintain transportation. Parallel developments include international cases reaching Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, and Canada; gene sequencing of the SARS coronavirus; WHO’s classification of outbreak regions; border restrictions; isolation measures; and early evidence affects universities, hospitals, and communities. Finally, it covers ongoing responses up to early May, addressing public communication, medical worker protections, exams and job fairs being postponed, and the introduction of dedicated SARS educational films.

nodes.title: **危机解除**[
nodes.summary: The excerpt describes the eradication of the SARS outbreak in China, focusing on actions from May to June 2003. It covers government responses such as Premier Wen Jiabao's emergency public health regulation and Beijing’s declaration of declining cases. It mentions key milestones in containment: hospitals like Beijing People's Hospital and Xiaotangshan hospital lifting quarantine, Beijing reaching zero new cases, and the closure of the SARS task force. It also notes WHO lifting travel warnings and a significant medical donation: 200,000 protective suits.

nodes.title: **疫情扑灭**[
nodes.summary: 该部分主要报道了2003至2004年严重急性呼吸综合征（SARS）疫情的消退过程及零星复发情况：先后有新加坡、香港、中国大陆、加拿大和台湾被世界卫生组织从疫区除名；2003年年底南方都市报声称广州再现SARS但未获官方证实；同年12月中华民国国防部研究所一名军官在实验室感染但未造成传染；2004年4月北京与安徽出现疑似病例并确认源自中国疾控中心病毒所的实验室感染。

nodes.title: **患者康复进度**[
nodes.summary: This section discusses how many SARS survivors suffered serious aftereffects, including bone necrosis that can cause disability, lung fibrosis, and mental health disorders such as depression. Some experts attribute the bone necrosis to the steroid treatments used during rescue efforts. In response, Beijing’s health authorities formed a specialist team in March 2004 to provide systematic care for patients with these sequelae. Despite government financial support, most still faced difficult living conditions, and roughly 60% of affected families experienced further hardships.

nodes.title: **对中国内地的影响**[
nodes.summary: The passage outlines how SARS affected mainland China, including strict rural community controls to prevent infected workers returning from Guangdong, disruptions to education leading to nationwide school closures and altered exam procedures, and cancellations or delays of major sporting events like the 2003 Chinese Jia-A League. It also discusses the central government’s increased investment in disease prevention infrastructure, support for traditional Chinese medicine in healthcare, and Guangdong’s legislation against consuming wild animals.

nodes.title: **对香港的影响**[
nodes.summary: The document describes how initial censorship of SARS information by the Chinese central government led to criticism for underestimating the outbreak’s risk, and how Hong Kong officials sought information from Guangdong while urging calm. Public dissatisfaction contributed to the massive 2003 July 1 protest, despite the CEPA agreement aimed at easing tensions. Hong Kong’s tourism sector was severely hit, prompting the introduction of the Individual Visit Scheme, which boosted the economy but also caused social issues such as parallel trading, high rents, discriminatory practices, hygiene problems, and deepened mainland-Hong Kong tensions.

nodes.title: **对欧美的影响**[
nodes.summary: The document segment describes how the SARS outbreak impacted international activities involving Europe and North America. It covers the relocation or cancellation of planned sports tournaments from China to countries like the U.S. and Italy, including major events such as FIFA’s Women’s World Cup, the World Women’s Ice Hockey Championships, and the World Women’s Volleyball Grand Prix. It also notes the broader economic consequences: layoffs in a European airline, declines in hotel occupancy and tourism in Guangdong, Hong Kong, and Chinese communities in North America, Swiss bans on Hong Kong participants in Zurich’s watch fair, and canceled conferences plus reduced hotel bookings in Toronto, Canada.

nodes.title: **对新加坡的影响**[
nodes.summary:
### **对新加坡的影响**[

[新加坡政府](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/新加坡政府)在3月27日宣布全国所有中小学校停课10天。由于担心疫情进一步扩散，政府在4月5日宣布分三阶段延长学校停课时间。所有初级学院将到4月9日复课，中学到4月14日复课，而小学和学前班则将到4月16日复课。

nodes.title: **疫情严重性评估检讨**[
nodes.summary: The partial document critiques assessments of SARS severity, presenting arguments that media and public reactions exaggerated its impact compared with other diseases. It cites statistics showing fewer global cases and deaths than common flu and notes SARS wasn’t among China’s top infection causes in 2003. Despite fears, China’s economy grew 8% that year. Counterarguments emphasize SARS was a novel, poorly understood virus affecting all age groups, making comparisons to seasonal flu inappropriate. The text also cautions against misleading epidemiological comparisons, advocating for proper metrics like case fatality rates and age-specific mortality rates to avoid errors such as Simpson’s paradox.

nodes.title: **香港防控措施检讨**[
nodes.summary: The document reviews Hong Kong’s response to the 2003 SARS outbreak, focusing on the severe impact of the epidemic, especially the Amoy Gardens cluster and the engineering factors that facilitated virus spread. It describes government measures such as mandatory mask-wearing in schools, temperature checks, school closures, and the move to online learning. The text also highlights public criticism of Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa’s administration—particularly Health Secretary Yeoh Eng-kiong—for failing to act decisively, prompting calls for accountability and contributing to the July 1 protest. Legislative investigation findings criticized Yeoh’s performance, leading to his eventual resignation. The document further covers the government’s multi-departmental investigation into the outbreak’s cause, noting structural issues in Hong Kong housing that exacerbated transmission, and concludes with an expert committee’s recognition that despite shortcomings, Hong Kong’s overall efforts ultimately controlled SARS.

nodes.title: **台湾防控措施检讨**[
nodes.summary: Section reviews Taiwan’s response to the 2003 SARS outbreak: outlines case numbers and deaths, legal classification of SARS, and citywide public health interventions. Focuses on Taipei’s Heping Hospital and the crisis caused by in-hospital transmission, the disputes between city and central health authorities over declaring SARS a notifiable disease, the media criticism of chaotic hospital lockdowns, and subsequent administrative resignations. Notes documentaries and books examining the incident and critiques of government strategy, particularly around mask distribution and legal designation of the disease.

nodes.title: **北京市疫情瞒报及相关争议**[
nodes.summary: The document segment discusses controversies around Beijing’s SARS case reporting: Health Minister Zhang Wenkang reported only 12 cases with 3 deaths, claiming SARS was controlled, but doctor Jiang Yanyong revealed much higher numbers from 309 Hospital and alerted media, leading to international exposure of Beijing’s outbreak. U.S. journalist Susan Jakes received Jiang’s email via a third party and published the information. Vice Health Minister Gao Qiang later defended Zhang and denied intentional concealment, citing communication difficulties and pointing to earlier Guangdong alerts; state media also criticized the Wall Street Journal’s report. On April 20, the Communist Party removed Zhang and deputy Beijing Party chief Meng Xuenong from their positions, with the national legislature formally dismissing Zhang as health minister.

nodes.title: **中国内地与香港关系相关争议**[
nodes.summary: The partial document details controversies around Hong Kong–mainland relations during and after the 2003 SARS outbreak. It recounts central government aid to Hong Kong, including donations of protective equipment, responses by Hong Kong officials like Donald Tsang and Tian Beijun, and debates over whether to accept or decline assistance. It highlights the 2014 “One Country, Two Systems” white paper’s portrayal of mainland support and economic measures such as CEPA and the “Individual Visit Scheme,” the resultant economic boost, and social tensions caused by increased mainland tourism. The document also notes criticisms from Hong Kong society and officials, arguing that SARS control relied primarily on Hong Kong’s medical professionals and pointing to initial delays in mainland reporting of the outbreak.

nodes.title: **台北市立和平医院封院**[
nodes.summary: Summary: The document describes the 2003 SARS outbreak at Taipei Municipal Hoping Hospital (now the Hoping branch of Taipei City Hospital), recounting how Mayor Ma Ying-jeou and Taipei city officials decided on an immediate lockdown with limited coordination, leading to controversy and strong enforcement rhetoric. It mentions Ma’s later reflection after nurse Chen Jing-Qiu’s death, and reports the outbreak’s toll: 57 staff infections, 7 staff deaths, 97 infections among people inside the hospital, and 24 deaths (including one suicide).
